chapter: Quality Serenaders, Cotton Club and union recollections
title: Sitting in with a white band, and the Chautauqua
summary: Collette asks about sitting in with a white band; Howard says he played solos as a guest, and starts to explain a Chautauqua.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Let's see, are we missing anybody else that we should ask about at this point? I think you mentioned on the other tape too something about -- it might be a repeat of something I asked you, but anyway, I guess it was at the Cotton Club, one of the clubs, where you happened to be there, and some white band, whether maybe it was Jimmy Dorsey, or I don't know who, you were invited to sit in, but as you know at that period it wasn't a general thing to have blacks and whites working together in clubs. But apparently, if you remember, you were able to come and sit in and they let you play and sort of walk on the stand and sort of join them. They wanted to hear Paul Howard, and Paul Howard wanted to work with them. But as far as the house policy it wasn't the thing to do. Do you remember anything about that?
I'm trying to think. I had a band. I had a thing I was playing, playing pieces with a white band.
Yeah. Apparently you knew the musicians well and they invited you over or something, but you either had to come through the stage entrance, the back door, and they let you come on and play, and --
I did. Yeah, that's true.
Do you remember who that was or where the club was or anything?
Steubenville, Ohio.
But it wasn't in Los Angeles that you did the same thing?
No. It wasn't in Los Angeles.
(Inaudible) [Off-mike]

I thought he did say that, yeah. You sure it wasn't the Cotton Club, because it seems like at the period, if I remember correctly, after you worked in Los Angeles, in other words you were working in Bullock's or somewhere, right? And you were a musician.
Yeah, I worked in Los Angeles.
What's that?
It could have been Los Angeles.
Yeah, it sounded like when you did meet these musicians they invited you over and I can't remember the name of the band now. Whether it's on the tape or not I don't

know. But it sounded like you went by, but, naturally, they let you come on and play, but you know, you just couldn't stay on the stand all evening. You played your solos and sort of walked back off. But anyway, it was just something I thought
Yeah, I walked off, didn't I. Played the solos and got off.
Yeah, you couldn't stay on, with the idea that you liked what they did and they liked what you did. But I think it was Los Angeles.
It was Los Angeles.
Are you sure it was the Cotton Club or something? Do you remember?
It wasn't the Cotton Club. It was -- it was -- I was just there as a guest, you know.
Right.
What do you call that thing? The -- it was a Chautauqua. You know what a Chautauqua is?
You told me once but I don't remember.
Well, it's where you have a band and you play by yourself and don't bother with nobody, and --
